items.stem: Which statement gives the law of conservation of mass?

options.text: No atoms are lost or made, so the products have the same mass as the reactants.
Mass stays the same only when the reaction is run inside a sealed vessel.
The number of molecules is unchanged, so the total mass cannot change.
Mass is conserved when a solid melts but not when it reacts chemically.

items.why: This is the law as the specification states it: the atom count is fixed, so the total mass is fixed.

items.stem: 8.0 g of magnesium is burned in an open crucible and 13.3 g of magnesium oxide is left. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The heat energy taken in during the burning has added 5.3 g to the solid.
5.3 g of oxygen from the air has joined the magnesium in the crucible.
Extra magnesium atoms have been made, which is why the mass rose.
The law of conservation of mass fails because the crucible is open.

items.why: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. The crucible is open, so oxygen enters and is weighed with the product: 13.3 - 8.0 = 5.3 g.

items.stem: A student writes H2 + O2 -> H2O and is told it is not balanced. Which change balances it correctly?

options.text: Change the product to H2O2 so that two oxygen atoms appear on the right.
Write a 2 in front of O2 so that four oxygen atoms become available.
Write a 2 in front of H2 and a 2 in front of H2O, leaving O2 alone.
Add one more oxygen atom to the right-hand side of the arrow.

items.why: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O gives four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side, changing only the multipliers.

items.stem: Why must a symbol equation be balanced?

options.text: So that the same number of molecules appears on both sides of the arrow.
So that the number of different substances shown matches on both sides.
So that the energy given out matches the energy taken in by the reaction.
No atoms are lost or made, so each element has equal atoms per side.

items.why: Balancing is the direct consequence of conservation of mass, stated in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element.

items.stem: In the formula 2Ca(NO3)2, what do the large 2 at the front and the small 2 after the bracket each do?

options.text: The front 2 shows two calcium atoms; the small 2 shows two nitrogen atoms.
The front 2 doubles the whole formula; the small 2 doubles the bracket only.
The front 2 doubles only the calcium; the small 2 doubles the oxygen.
Both 2s multiply every atom, so each count in the formula is doubled twice.

items.why: A multiplier in normal script applies to the entire formula unit; a subscript after a bracket applies to the bracketed group.

items.stem: Calculate the relative formula mass of Ca(OH)2. Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1.

options.text: 57, from adding 40, 16 and 1 with the bracket subscript ignored.
58, from doubling the hydrogen atoms but keeping one oxygen.
74, because the bracket doubles both the oxygen and the hydrogen.
114, from doubling every atom in the formula, the calcium included.

items.why: Mr = 40 + 2(16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74, the sum of the relative atomic masses in the numbers shown.

items.stem: The relative atomic mass of oxygen is 16. What is the relative formula mass of O2?

options.text: 16, since that is the relative atomic mass given for oxygen.
16, since writing O2 does not add any mass to the oxygen.
18, from adding 16 to the 2 written in the formula.
32, because the molecule contains two atoms of oxygen.

items.why: Mr is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown: 2 x 16 = 32.

items.stem: For 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO the reactants total (2 x 24) + 32 = 80. The Mr of MgO is 40. What is the product total?

options.text: 80, since the same atoms are present on each side.
40, because the relative formula mass of MgO is 40.
64, because the 2 in front multiplies only the magnesium.
48, because only the magnesium ends up in the solid.

items.why: The quantity shown is 2MgO, so 2 x 40 = 80, equal to the reactant total as a balanced equation requires.

items.stem: Ammonium nitrate is NH4NO3, with Mr = 80. The relative atomic mass of nitrogen is 14. What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen?

options.text: 22%, from the 2 nitrogen atoms among the 9 atoms in the formula.
17.5%, from using the mass of only one of the nitrogen atoms.
35%, because the two nitrogen atoms give 28 out of the total of 80.
70%, from doubling for the two nitrogen atoms a second time.

items.why: (2 x 14) / 80 x 100 = 35%, using the relative formula mass and relative atomic mass supplied.

items.stem: Which method gives the percentage by mass of an element in a compound?

options.text: Divide the number of atoms of that element by the total atoms, then x 100.
Divide the Mr of the compound by the Ar of that element, then x 100.
Divide the Ar of the element by the Mr of the compound, then x 100.
Multiply the Ar by the number of those atoms, divide by Mr, then x 100.

items.why: The standard route, using the relative formula mass and relative atomic masses the question supplies.

items.stem: A weighed piece of copper is heated in an open crucible. The mass of the solid increases. Why?

options.text: Oxygen from the air has combined with the copper to form copper oxide.
Heat energy absorbed from the flame has added to the mass of the metal.
The copper atoms expand as they get hot, so each one becomes much heavier.
New copper atoms are made as the reaction goes on in the crucible.

items.why: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. The oxide is heavier than the metal because the oxygen taken from the air is now weighed with it.

items.stem: Copper carbonate is heated in an open test tube: CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2. The mass of the solid falls. Why?

options.text: Some of the solid has been burned away by the heat of the Bunsen flame.
Carbon dioxide escapes, leaving copper oxide as the solid.
Mass is lost from the tube, so mass is not conserved in this reaction.
Strong heating has destroyed some of the solid, so that part no longer exists.

items.why: In the thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate the carbon dioxide escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.

items.stem: Use the particle model to explain why the balance reading falls when a metal carbonate is heated in an open tube.

options.text: The particles left in the tube move further apart, so the solid weighs less than before.
Gas particles carry no mass of their own, so the reading falls as gas forms.
Particles are destroyed as the solid turns into a gas inside the hot tube.
Carbon dioxide particles leave the tube and mix into the air, so they are no longer weighed.

items.why: The particle-model account the specification asks for: the particles still exist, but they are no longer inside the system on the balance.

items.stem: A student reads 25.00 cm3 from a burette, working carefully. Which statement about that measurement is correct?

options.text: There is always some uncertainty about the result, however careful you are.
There is no uncertainty, because a burette is precise apparatus.
Uncertainty appears only if the student misreads the burette scale.
Uncertainty would disappear if the whole titration were repeated three times.

items.why: Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained.

items.stem: Five titres are 24.8, 25.0, 25.1, 25.0 and 27.4 cm3. How should this set of results be handled?

options.text: Include all five in the mean, because a measured result may never be dropped.
Plot all five, treat 27.4 as anomalous and leave it out of the mean.
Just take the mean and treat it as the exact result, since averaging removes any doubt.
Use a single titre, since a precise burette gives the exact volume.

items.why: Representing the distribution shows 27.4 lying well away from the cluster, which is how an anomaly is identified.

items.stem: Four titres have a mean of 25.0 cm3, a lowest value of 24.8 cm3 and a highest of 25.2 cm3. How should the result be quoted?

options.text: 25.0 plus or minus 0.4 cm3, quoting the whole range as the uncertainty.
Report all four titres separately, since no reading may be left out.
25.0 plus or minus 0.2 cm3, which is half the range of 0.4 cm3.
25.0 cm3 exactly, since averaging the titres removes the uncertainty.

items.why: The range 25.2 - 24.8 = 0.4 cm3 is used about the mean, so the uncertainty quoted is half of it.

items.stem: A bottle in a laboratory is labelled '0.50 mol of sodium chloride'. What does the '0.50 mol' tell you?

options.text: the chemical amount of sodium chloride present
the mass of the sodium chloride, in grams
the number of sodium ions in the bottle
the volume the sodium chloride fills

items.why: Chemical amounts are measured in moles and mol is the symbol for that unit, so the label states an amount of substance.

items.stem: The relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, is 100. What is the mass of one mole of calcium carbonate?

options.text: 1 g

items.why: The mass of one mole in grams is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, so one mole of CaCO₃ has a mass of 100 g.

items.stem: One mole of water, H₂O (Mr = 18), has a smaller mass than one mole of sulfur dioxide, SO₂ (Mr = 64). Why?

options.text: water is a liquid while sulfur dioxide is a gas
one mole of water contains fewer molecules
the relative formula mass of water is smaller
water molecules are packed more closely

items.why: The mass of one mole in grams is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, and 18 is less than 64.

items.stem: A sample holds one mole of magnesium atoms. Another sample holds one mole of helium atoms. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The magnesium sample contains more atoms than the helium.
The helium sample contains more atoms, as it is lighter.
The two samples must have the same mass as each other.
The two samples contain the same number of atoms.

items.why: One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles as one mole of any other substance.

items.stem: What is the value of the Avogadro constant?

options.text: 6.02 x 10²³ particles in one mole
6.02 x 10²² particles in a mole
6.02 x 10²³ particles per gram
6.02 x 10²³ g for every mole

items.why: The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole.

items.stem: What does the Avogadro constant tell you?

options.text: the number of particles in one gram of any substance
the number of particles in one mole of a substance
the number of moles in one gram of a substance
the mass in grams of one mole of a substance

items.why: The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance is the Avogadro constant.

items.stem: In one mole of carbon (C) the number of atoms is the same as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂). How many moles of atoms are there in one mole of CO₂?

options.text: one mole of atoms, as this is one mole of substance
44 moles of atoms, from its relative formula mass
three moles of atoms, one carbon and two oxygen
two moles of atoms, one for each element present

items.why: Each CO₂ molecule holds three atoms, so one mole of molecules contains three moles of atoms.

items.stem: Which statement about amounts in moles is correct?

options.text: One mole of any solid contains 6.02 x 10²³ atoms.
Moles can count atoms but not electrons or ions.
One mole of CO₂ contains one mole of atoms in total.
One mole of MgCl₂ contains three moles of ions.

items.why: Amounts in moles apply to ions as well as atoms and molecules: one mole of MgCl₂ gives one mole of Mg²⁺ and two moles of Cl⁻.

items.stem: How many moles are there in 20 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ (Mr = 100)?

options.text: 0.20 mol
5.0 mol
20 mol
2 mol

items.why: number of moles = mass ÷ Mr = 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20 mol.

items.stem: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂ (Mr = 95)?
items.why: mass = number of moles x Mr = 0.25 x 95 = 23.75 g.

items.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. In a sealed container, 4.8 g of magnesium reacts completely with 3.2 g of oxygen. Which statement about the magnesium oxide formed is correct?

options.text: It is less than 8.0 g, as some mass is lost as gas.
It is 4.8 g, since only the magnesium is weighed out.
It is 8.0 g, the total mass of the reactants.
It is 3.2 g, the mass of the oxygen that reacted.

items.why: Mass is conserved in a closed system, so 4.8 g + 3.2 g of reactants give 8.0 g of magnesium oxide.

items.stem: The equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O can be interpreted in terms of moles. Which reading of it is correct?

options.text: Two grams of H₂ react with one gram of O₂ gas.
H₂ and O₂ react in a 2 : 1 ratio by mass.
Two molecules of H₂ give one molecule of H₂O.
Two moles of H₂ react with one mole of O₂.

items.why: The balancing numbers give the amounts in moles: two moles of hydrogen to one mole of oxygen.

items.stem: The equation Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ is given in the specification. Which statement does it show?

options.text: One mole of Mg reacts with two moles of HCl.
A gram of Mg reacts with two grams of HCl.
The masses of Mg and HCl are in a 1 : 2 ratio.
One mole of Mg needs two grams of HCl.

items.why: The balancing numbers show one mole of magnesium reacting with two moles of hydrochloric acid.

items.stem: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What mass of magnesium chloride (Mr = 95) is produced when 2.4 g of magnesium (Ar = 24) reacts completely?
items.why: 2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.1 mol of Mg, which gives 0.1 mol of MgCl₂, and 0.1 x 95 = 9.5 g.

items.stem: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What mass of calcium oxide (Mr = 56) is produced when 25 g of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) decomposes completely?
items.why: 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol of CaCO₃ gives 0.25 mol of CaO, and 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.

items.stem: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What mass of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) must be heated to produce 5.6 g of calcium oxide (Mr = 56)?
items.why: 5.6 ÷ 56 = 0.1 mol of CaO, so 0.1 mol of CaCO₃ is needed, and 0.1 x 100 = 10 g.

items.stem: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, one mole of nitrogen reacts with three moles of hydrogen. Why is the mass of hydrogen used not three times the mass of nitrogen?

options.text: the balancing numbers give a ratio of moles, not of masses
the mass ratio is the same as the mole ratio in all cases
some of the hydrogen escapes before it is able to react
hydrogen must have more mass, as it has more molecules

items.why: Each amount must be converted to a mass using its own relative formula mass, so the mass ratio is 6 g to 28 g.

items.stem: The masses of the reactants and products in a reaction are known. How are the balancing numbers in the symbol equation found?

options.text: use the ratio of the masses in grams as the numbers
convert each mass to moles, then find the simplest ratio
divide each mass by the first element's relative atomic mass
multiply each mass by its relative formula mass

items.why: Masses in grams are converted to amounts in moles, and those amounts are converted to simple whole number ratios.

items.stem: 4.0 g of hydrogen (Mr of H₂ = 2), 32 g of oxygen (Mr of O₂ = 32) and 36 g of water (Mr of H₂O = 18) are measured in a reaction. Which balanced equation fits these masses?

options.text: 4H₂ + 2O₂ → 4H₂O
4H₂ + 32O₂ → 36H₂O
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
H₂ + O₂ → H₂O

items.why: 4.0 ÷ 2 = 2 mol H₂, 32 ÷ 32 = 1 mol O₂ and 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol H₂O, a ratio of 2 : 1 : 2.

items.stem: 2.4 g of magnesium (Ar = 24) reacts with 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid (Mr of HCl = 36.5) to give 9.5 g of magnesium chloride (Mr = 95) and 0.2 g of hydrogen (Mr of H₂ = 2). Which equation fits these masses?

options.text: 2Mg + 4HCl → 2MgCl₂ + 2H₂
2.4Mg + 7.3HCl → 9.5MgCl₂ + 0.2H₂
Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

items.why: 0.1 mol Mg, 0.2 mol HCl, 0.1 mol MgCl₂ and 0.1 mol H₂ give the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 : 1.

items.stem: The amount of a substance is found from number of moles = mass ÷ Mr. To make mass the subject of this relationship, what should you do?

options.text: Multiply the number of moles by the Mr.
Multiply the mass by the number of moles.
Divide the Mr by the number of moles.
Divide the number of moles by Mr.

items.why: Multiplying both sides by Mr leaves mass on its own, giving mass = number of moles x Mr.

items.stem: Concentration = mass of solute ÷ volume of solution. A student knows the concentration and the volume and needs the mass of solute. What should they do?

options.text: Multiply the concentration by 1000 cm³ first.
Multiply the concentration by the volume.
Divide the concentration by the volume used.
Divide the volume by the concentration.

items.why: Multiplying both sides by the volume makes the mass of solute the subject.

items.stem: In a reaction between two reactants, what is meant by the limiting reactant?

options.text: the reactant that is added in excess
the reactant with the smallest mass used
the reactant that is completely used up
the reactant that is left over at the end

items.why: The reactant that is completely used up is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products.

items.stem: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. A student adds 0.10 mol of magnesium to 0.10 mol of hydrochloric acid. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The magnesium is limiting, as it has the smaller mass.
Neither reactant is limiting, as the amounts match.
The magnesium is the limiting reactant in this mixture.
The hydrochloric acid is the limiting reactant.

items.why: 0.10 mol of Mg needs 0.20 mol of HCl, so the acid runs out first and the magnesium is in excess.

items.stem: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 0.20 mol of magnesium is burned in 0.50 mol of oxygen. Which statement is correct?

options.text: 0.20 mol of MgO forms, as the magnesium is limiting
0.50 mol of MgO forms, since the oxygen is in excess
2 mol of MgO forms, straight from the equation
0.10 mol of MgO forms, from the 2 in the equation

items.why: 0.20 mol of Mg needs only 0.10 mol of O₂, so the magnesium is used up and gives 0.20 mol of MgO.

items.stem: A reaction is repeated with twice as much of the limiting reactant, while the other reactant is still in excess. What happens to the maximum mass of product?

options.text: It stays the same, as the equation fixes the amount formed.
It doubles, as the limiting reactant sets the amount formed.
It halves, because the excess reactant is now shared out.
It is unchanged until the excess reactant is doubled.

items.why: The amount of product is proportional to the amount of the limiting reactant while the other is in excess.

items.stem: A solution has a concentration of 20 g/dm³. What does this tell you?

options.text: there is 20 g of solute in each 1 cm³ of solution
there is 20 g of solute, whatever the volume may be
there is 20 g of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution
any solution holding 20 g of solute has this concentration

items.why: Concentration measured in g/dm³ is a mass per given volume of solution, here 20 g in each dm³.

items.stem: A solution has a concentration of 12 g/dm³. What mass of solute is present in 250 cm³ of this solution?
items.why: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³, and mass = concentration x volume = 12 x 0.25 = 3.0 g.

items.stem: A student needs 7.5 g of a solute. The solution available has a concentration of 25 g/dm³. What volume of the solution should be measured out?

options.text: 300 cm³
0.30 cm³
30 cm³

items.why: volume = mass ÷ concentration = 7.5 ÷ 25 = 0.3 dm³, and 0.3 x 1000 = 300 cm³.

items.stem: A solution contains 4.0 g of solute in 200 cm³ of solution. Water is added until the volume of the solution is 400 cm³. What happens to the concentration?

options.text: It rises from 20 g/dm³ to 40 g/dm³, as more has been added.
It falls from 20 g/dm³ to 10 g/dm³, as the volume doubles.
It stays at 20 g/dm³, as the mass of solute is fixed.
It falls from 2.0 g/dm³ to 1.0 g/dm³, halving as water goes in.

items.why: The mass of solute stays at 4.0 g while the volume doubles to 0.4 dm³, so 4.0 ÷ 0.4 = 10 g/dm³.
